newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Observers say Romanian elections free and fair.
newsitem.headline: Observers say Romanian elections free and fair.

text.p: Romania's general election was free and fair despite problems with its organisation, international observers who watched over polling said on Monday.

"As far as we can see now, Romania had free elections, reasonably fair and transparent, but with transparency still needing improvement," Geza Jeszenszky, head of a Council of Europe delegation, told a news conference.
"There was no intimidation or undue influence."
A delegation from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe said earlier on Monday that its members had reached the same conclusion.

But Jeszenszky, a former Hungarian foreign minister, said the delegation was concerned about errors in voting lists, parallel "special lists" that allowed unregistered voters to cast ballots and the poor quality of ballot paper.
Members also suggested improvements could be made in vote-counting techniques, now mainly done by hand.

First results give the opposition Democratic Convention (CDR) a big lead over ex-communists in Sunday's poll. Incumbent Ion Iliescu has a three-point lead over his CDR opponent in the presidential race, which will go to a run-off later this month.
In the run-up to the parliamentary and presidential elections, opposition parties had expressed fears of mass vote-rigging by the ruling ex-communists, who have been in power since 1989.
The final stage of the campaign was complicated by a decision to reprint some 3.5 million ballots two days before the vote because of errors.
Romanian media reported several irregularities in Sunday's voting, but there appeared to be no evidence of massive fraud.

The daily Romania Libera complained that electoral lists had sometimes contained people who had died or moved away from their districts. Ziua newspaper reported that some voters were handed ballots with one candidate clearly marked.
Jeszenszky said there were some improvements since the last general election in 1992. Those polls were also deemed "reasonably free and relatively fair" by the Council of Europe.
